## Project Overview

ClaudeKit Marketing is a comprehensive toolkit for sales and marketing automation using Claude Code subagent orchestration. This toolkit enables autonomous marketing workflows for content creation, campaign management, SEO optimization, and lead generation.

**Target Users:** Indie hackers, small marketing teams, SMB marketing managers

## What We're Building (CRITICAL)

**The deliverable is the `$HOME/.claude/` folder itself** - a reusable kit users install in THEIR projects.

```
OUTPUT: ./claudekit-marketing/.claude/

        ├── skills/      # Domain knowledge

        └── hooks/       # Automation hooks
```

# Skill Workflow Routing

Use this file to choose capabilities, not command names. Resolve each bracketed
capability against the runtime's live installed-skill catalog before invoking
anything. Skip optional capabilities that are unavailable; never synthesize an
absent skill command.

## Core Development Workflow

```text
[brainstorm] -> [plan] -> [implement] -> [test] -> [review] -> [ship] -> [journal]
```

- New feature: start with the brainstorm contract, then plan and implement.
- Accepted plan: reuse its outcome, constraints, non-goals, and acceptance
  criteria before implementation.
- Quick change: keep the brainstorm gate bounded, then use the fastest installed
  implementation workflow that still verifies the result.

## Bugfix Workflow

```text
[frame outcome] -> [scout] -> [diagnose] -> [choose fix] -> [implement] -> [test] -> [review]
```

- Prove the cause before changing behavior.
- Read-only investigation may stop after scouting or diagnosis.
- If no specialized debugging skill is installed, use native read and test
  capabilities without inventing a skill invocation.

## Investigation Workflow

```text
[scout] -> [diagnose] -> [brainstorm options when needed] -> [plan when delivery follows]
```

An investigation does not require a design approval loop unless it turns into
delivery work.

## Post-Implementation Capabilities

After implementation, use installed capabilities for:

- code review before merge;
- release or shipping validation when publication is in scope;
- decision or journal capture when the repository requires it.

## Shared-Workspace Setup

After the opening brainstorm contract and before implementation, use an
installed worktree/isolation capability when the repository workflow requires
one. Use an installed scouting capability or native file search to discover
relevant patterns.

Route domain work from the runtime's live installed-skill catalog. Kit
composition can replace an entire skill set, so a copied command inventory in
this shared rule is never authoritative.

1. Read the live skill catalog supplied by the runtime.
2. Match the user's primary intent to a capability below.
3. Select an installed skill whose metadata explicitly covers that capability.
4. Read that skill's complete instructions before acting.

# Development Rules

Use this file when editing code, tests, scripts, or configuration.

## Baseline

- Follow project docs in `docs/` and existing local patterns.
- Apply KISS and DRY. Deliver the full requested scope — do not trim, defer, or
  simplify away features the user explicitly asked for. Add nothing beyond the
  request. When the user passes `--yagni`, additionally apply YAGNI (You Aren't
  Gonna Need It): challenge and cut any scope not needed for the stated outcome.
- Implement real behavior. Do not add fake data, mocks, or temporary shortcuts just to satisfy a check.
- Keep changes scoped to the request and the affected contracts.
- Use descriptive kebab-case file names for new files when the repo has no stronger convention.
- Split code only when it reduces real complexity or matches existing module boundaries.

## Quality Gates

- Run the narrowest useful test first, then broaden when shared behavior or public contracts changed.
- Do not hide failing tests, lint, type, build, or syntax errors.
- Preserve public contracts unless the change intentionally updates them and the user accepted that scope.
- Keep commits focused and use conventional commit format without AI references.
- Never commit secrets, dotenv files, tokens, private keys, database credentials, or personal data.

## Tooling

- Use `gh` for GitHub operations when needed.
- Use current docs only when the API/tooling may have changed.
- Use relevant skills by reading their descriptions first, then opening only the needed `SKILL.md`.
- Use `/ak:preview` only when a visual explanation will materially help the user understand the change.

# Orchestration Protocol

Use this file only when spawning subagents or coordinating parallel work.

## Delegation Context

Every subagent prompt should include:

- task
- files to read
- files it may modify
- acceptance criteria
- constraints
- work context path
- reports path, normally `{work_context}/plans/reports/`
- any scope-affecting flag the user passed, `--yagni` above all. A delegate that
  never sees the flag silently reverts to the default of delivering the full
  requested scope.

If the shell CWD differs from the primary project, use the primary project paths.

## Context Isolation

- Do not pass full conversation history.
- Summarize only decisions needed for the subtask.
- Give exact file paths instead of "look around the repo" unless scouting is the task.
- Keep coordination, merge decisions, and user approvals in the controller session.

## Parallel Work

Use parallel subagents only when file ownership is clear and integration points are known. Avoid parallel edits to the same file, generated artifact, database migration sequence, or shared config.

## Status Protocol

Ask subagents to end with:

```text
Status: DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
Summary: one or two sentences
Concerns/Blockers: optional
```

Handle `BLOCKED` and `NEEDS_CONTEXT` by changing context, scope, or approach. Do not retry the same failing prompt repeatedly.

## Model Escalation

When the current session or a subagent runs on a model below `fable` (e.g. `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku`) and hits a hard problem — repeated failed attempts, a high-stakes design fork, or fuzzy requirements — spawn the `kongming` agent for counsel instead of switching the session model. `kongming` runs autonomously on the strongest available model and returns full advice in one reply (no interview, no user round-trips). Give it the task, evidence gathered so far, approaches tried, and the specific question. It advises only; the caller stays responsible for the implementation. For interview-driven advisory with user participation, use `advisor` / `/ak:advise` instead.

For multi-session team work, use `/ak:team` and its skill-local rules.

# Review, Audit, and Decision Rules

Use this file when reviewing code, applying audit feedback, or cutting scope.

## Verified Decisions

Once a decision is verified by source, tests, or an empirical check, do not reverse it because an audit raises an abstract concern. Reverse only when the audit adds new evidence or the context changed.

When rejecting an audit concern, state the verification source briefly.

## User Decisions

Do not silently undo explicit user decisions. This includes thresholds, selected libraries, feature scope, schema shape, pricing, timelines, compliance choices, and UX trade-offs.

If an audit suggests reversing a user decision, present:

- the original decision
- the audit concern
- the trade-off
- the concrete options

Then wait for the user.

## Threat Model

Before applying a security or robustness finding, identify what the code actually stores, protects, or exposes. Fix real failure modes. Document non-issues briefly. Ask when the risk is plausible but depends on product intent.

## Scout First

For questions answerable by reading the repo, scout before asking. Ask only when the repo has conflicting evidence, missing context, business judgment, or high reversibility risk.

## Stable Code Artifacts

Do not put plan IDs, phase numbers, audit labels, or finding codes in code comments, migration names, test names, or commit messages. Explain the invariant or behavior directly.

# Process and Resource Management

Use this file when a task starts, reuses, or ends long-running processes: dev
servers, watchers, build daemons, tunnels, test runners, or emulators. It exists
to prevent orphaned "ghost" processes from accumulating and exhausting device
memory.

## The failure mode

Agents start a dev environment, then abandon it. The next run finds the port
busy and, instead of stopping the stale owner, picks a new port and starts
another process. Repeat, and the machine fills with duplicate processes and
held ports. Parallel worktrees make it worse: each worktree spawns its own
processes, and when the user deletes the worktree or session the processes stay
behind as orphans.

## Rules

- Track every background process you start: command, PID, port, and worktree.
  Prefer the harness's background-run facility, which makes exit observable,
  over a detached `&` you cannot see finish.
- Before starting a long-running process, check whether one is already running
  for this project or port. Reuse or stop it; do not spawn a duplicate.
- Bind to a deterministic port per project/worktree. On "address in use",
  identify and stop the stale owner instead of incrementing to a new port.
  Inspect with `lsof -i :PORT` / `ss -ltnp` on macOS/Linux, `netstat -ano` on
  Windows.
- Stop what you started when its task, session, or worktree ends. Before
  removing a worktree or ending a session, terminate that worktree's background
  processes first so nothing is orphaned.
- Reconcile periodically: list your running dev processes (`ps`, `lsof`) and
  stop the ones that no longer map to an active task or worktree.
- Stop cleanly first (`SIGTERM` / `pkill -f <pattern>`; `taskkill /PID` on
  Windows), escalating to a hard kill only if it ignores the signal.

## Safety

Only stop processes you started or clearly own. Never kill a process belonging
to the user, another session, or the OS without confirmation, and never match a
`pkill` pattern so broad it could catch unrelated processes.

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- advisor: Use this agent to run the interview-driven `ak:advise` advisory workflow in an isolated context on the strongest available model. It scouts, interviews the user one question at a time to reframe a raw idea into exact requirements and goals, then delivers honest advice (what to do, what to avoid, better alternatives, benefits, trade-offs, a work checklist, and success metrics). Because a Claude Code subagent cannot call `AskUserQuestion` itself, this agent relays each interview question back to the orchestrator and is re-spawned with the user's answer. Examples: - <example>
    Context: User wants an unbiased second opinion before committing to a design.
    user: "Should I build my own job queue or use an off-the-shelf one?"
    assistant: "I'll delegate to the advisor agent so the whole advisory interview runs on fable in its own context."
    <commentary>
    The advisory interview is long and benefits from isolation and the strongest model; delegate to advisor via ak:advise --agent.
    </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
    Context: A workflow (ak:plan, ak:vibe) reaches a decision point that needs honest advisory reframing.
    user: "The requirements feel fuzzy — what should we actually build here?"
    assistant: "Let me spawn the advisor agent to reframe this into exact requirements and goals before we plan."
    <commentary>
    advisor is a reusable advisory step other skills can invoke mid-workflow.
    </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskUpdate, TaskList, SendMessage, Task(Explore), Edit)
- analytics-analyst: Use this agent for performance reporting and marketing insights. This includes campaign performance reports, traffic analysis, conversion tracking, custom event analysis, and trend identification. Examples:

user: "Generate a monthly marketing performance report"
assistant: "I'll use the analytics-analyst agent to create your performance report"
</example>

<example>

- attraction-specialist: Use this agent for lead generation, top-of-funnel content, and competitor intelligence. This includes keyword research, gap analysis, landing page content, programmatic SEO templates, and lead magnet ideation. Examples:

- brainstormer: Use this agent when you need to brainstorm software solutions, evaluate architectural approaches, or debate technical decisions before implementation. Examples: - <example>

    </commentary>
  </example>

- <example>

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## 00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## codegraph
# Codegraph — available (per-project; pass projectPath)

Codegraph is a SQLite knowledge graph of a codebase's symbols, edges, and
files: one `codegraph_explore` call returns the verbatim, line-numbered source
of the relevant symbols PLUS the call paths between them and a blast-radius
summary — replacing a grep + Read loop with one round-trip.

This server started somewhere with no `.codegraph/` of its own, so there is no
default project — but the tools are available and work **per project**:

- To query a project that HAS a `.codegraph/` index (e.g. a service inside a
  monorepo, or a second repo), pass its path as `projectPath` to
  `codegraph_explore` (and any other codegraph tool). Codegraph resolves the
  nearest `.codegraph/` at or above that path and answers from it — for as many
  projects as you like in one session.
- For a project with no `.codegraph/`, use your built-in tools (Read/Grep/Glob)
  for that project. Indexing is the user's decision — don't run it yourself, but
  if it comes up they can run `codegraph init` in a project to enable codegraph
  there (a new index is picked up live, no restart).

OpenBox Logger is a local, reversible observation stack for authorized **Claude Desktop Code — Local** sessions. It keeps three evidence lanes separate:

1. Claude's plaintext JSONL transcripts: persisted messages, tool calls, tool results, and subagent records.
2. Claude Code OpenTelemetry: prompts, model requests, permission decisions, tool/MCP events, metrics, traces, and opt-in raw Messages API bodies.
3. Optional mitmproxy TLS inspection: the actual `api.anthropic.com` HTTP request and streaming response transport.

It does not claim to expose hidden reasoning, server-internal processing, local IPC, or cloud-session execution. See [Capture model](docs/CAPTURE_MODEL.md).

## Safety defaults

- Listeners bind only to `127.0.0.1`.
- The proxy intercepts only `api.anthropic.com`; other hosts pass without TLS inspection.
- Proxy credentials and cookies are redacted before events are persisted.
- No system-wide CA is installed. Claude trusts the project CA only through `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` while capture settings are active.
- Existing transcripts are skipped when a run starts. Historical import requires an explicit `--yes`.
- Claude settings activation fails on conflicting values, saves exact backups, and restores only keys it manages.
- Starting the stack does not edit Claude settings or restart Claude Desktop.
- Captures under `data/` are private and excluded from Git.

Raw transcripts and API bodies can still contain source code, credentials, personal data, and command output. Read [Security](docs/SECURITY.md) before enabling capture.

## Quick start

Requirements: macOS, Claude Desktop, Docker Desktop, and Python 3.11 or later.

```bash
make init
make doctor
make start-proxy
make enable-proxy
```

Then fully quit and reopen Claude Desktop and start a new **Local** session in the Code tab. Capture only begins for new transcript records; it does not import earlier conversations.

```bash
./bin/openbox-logger status
./bin/openbox-logger tail --source transcript
./bin/openbox-logger tail --source proxy
./bin/openbox-logger report
./bin/openbox-logger snapshot
```

When finished:

```bash
make disable
make stop
```

Quit and reopen Claude Desktop again after disabling. Captured data and settings backups remain under `data/` until you deliberately remove them.

## Capture without TLS interception

The native transcript and OpenTelemetry lanes are normally sufficient and avoid running a TLS proxy:

```bash
make start
make enable
```

This is the recommended default when transport-level evidence is not required.

## Commands

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `init` | Creates private data directories. |
| `doctor` | Checks Docker, Claude Desktop, transcripts, and settings without mutation. |
| `start [--proxy]` | Starts the collector, future-only transcript watcher, and optional proxy. |
| `enable [--proxy]` | Adds capture variables to `~/.claude/settings.json` with a backup. |
| `status` | Reports watcher, collector, proxy, run, and activation state. |
| `tail` | Shows recent normalized transcript or proxy events. |
| `report` | Reports file sizes and event counts without message content. |
| `snapshot` | Produces a SHA-256 manifest of captured files. |
| `export-redacted` | Creates a derived field- and token-redacted export; raw data is unchanged. |
| `import-history --yes` | Explicitly imports existing Claude transcripts. |
| `disable` | Restores only settings keys owned by the active capture. |
| `stop` | Stops this project's watcher and containers; data is retained. |

Run `./bin/openbox-logger <command> --help` for options.

## Data layout

```text
data/
├── api-bodies/                 Untruncated Messages API request/response JSON
├── backups/                    Exact Claude settings backups
├── exports/                    Snapshots and derived redacted exports
├── mitmproxy/                  Project-only proxy CA and keys
├── runs/<run-id>/
│   ├── otel/                   OTLP logs, traces, and metrics
│   ├── proxy/events.jsonl      Redacted-header transport events and bodies
│   ├── transcripts/events.jsonl
│   └── run.json
└── state/                      Activation and current-run state
```

The collector uses official pinned images:

- `otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.156.0`
- `mitmproxy/mitmproxy:12.2.3`

```bash
make test
make validate
```

`validate` compiles the Python modules, validates Compose, and asks the pinned Collector binary to validate its own configuration. It does not enable Claude capture.

# Capture model

## Scope

This project observes authorized Claude Desktop **Code tab, Local environment** sessions. Cloud and SSH sessions require observation at their execution host and are not qualified by a proxy on this Mac.

```text
Claude Desktop Code UI
        │ local IPC (not captured by proxy)
        ▼
embedded Claude Code engine
        ├── JSONL transcript ───────────────► normalized transcript events
        ├── OTLP logs/traces/metrics ───────► local Collector files
        ├── raw API-body telemetry ─────────► untruncated request/response JSON
        ├── local tools and stdio MCP ──────► transcript + OTel after execution
        └── HTTPS api.anthropic.com ────────► optional mitmproxy transport events
```

## Coverage

| Signal | Transcript | OTel/raw body | Proxy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User prompt | Yes | Yes | Yes, when sent to API |
| Client-side system prompt and tools | Partial | Yes, raw request | Yes, raw request |
| Assistant response | Yes, assembled | Yes, assembled | Yes, raw SSE transport |
| Tool call/result returned to model | Yes | Yes | Yes, on later API body |
| Local tool execution detail | Returned output only | Structured events/content | Only network egress honoring proxy |
| Permission accept/reject | Not authoritative | `tool_decision` event | No |
| MCP stdio exchange | Result in transcript | MCP/tool events | No |
| API retries/transport errors | Partial | Per-attempt events | Yes |
| Hidden extended thinking | No | Redacted by Claude | No usable plaintext guarantee |
| Desktop UI-only state | No | No | No |
| Server-internal processing | No | No | No |

No individual lane is treated as “all messages.” A complete local observation combines transcript persistence, OTel event evidence, and—only when needed—transport capture.

## Correlation

- `session_id` ties transcript, OTel, and proxy records to a Claude session.
- `X-Claude-Code-Session-Id` is retained in proxy events while authentication headers are redacted.
- `request_id` ties a successful proxy response to API and OTel response records when Anthropic returns it.
- `flow_id`, transcript `source_file`/`source_offset`, and OTel `event.sequence` preserve lane-local ordering.
- Snapshot manifests bind retained files by path, byte count, and SHA-256.

## Freshness and historical data

At run start, the watcher records the end offset of every existing transcript. Only later appends and newly created transcript files are copied into the run. `import-history --yes` is a separate, explicit operation.
=== docs/SCHEMA.md ===
# Event schema

Normalized transcript and proxy records use `openbox.desktop-observation/v1` and are stored as newline-delimited JSON.

## Common fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema` | Closed schema identifier. |
| `observed_at` | UTC observation time generated by OpenBox Logger. |
| `source` | `claude_transcript` or `mitmproxy`. |
| `kind` | Lane-specific event type. |
| `session_id` | Claude Code session identifier when available. |

## Transcript events

Transcript records additionally contain:

- `source_file`: path relative to `~/.claude/projects`, never the absolute home path.
- `source_offset`: byte offset of the original JSONL record.
- `payload`: the complete parsed Claude transcript object.
- `kind`: `transcript.<payload.type>`.

Invalid JSON is retained as `transcript.invalid_json` with `raw` and `parse_error`.

## Proxy events

`proxy.request` contains `flow_id`, method, sanitized URL, redacted headers, and the full request body. `proxy.response` contains the same correlation identifiers plus status, Anthropic request ID, redacted headers, and the full assembled response transport body. `proxy.error` records transport failures.

Bodies are encoded as:

```json
{
  "encoding": "json | utf-8 | base64 | none",
  "value": {},
  "bytes": 123
}
```

## OTel files

Collector output remains canonical OTLP JSON rather than being projected into the OpenBox event schema. This preserves all upstream resource, scope, log, metric, and trace fields. The file exporter's JSON shape is an upstream alpha contract and may change when the pinned collector is upgraded.
=== docs/SECURITY.md ===
# Security and data handling

OpenBox Logger deliberately collects highly sensitive developer data. Operate it only for accounts, projects, and sessions you are authorized to observe.

## Raw data

The following are intentionally unredacted because they are evidence sources:

- Claude transcript payloads.
- `OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES=file:...` request and response files.
- OTel tool content when Claude emits it.
- Proxy request and response bodies.

They can contain complete conversation history, file contents, shell output, MCP results, URLs, and credentials accidentally exposed to Claude. Files are created under `data/` with private directory permissions where the host process controls creation. Docker Desktop remains part of the local trust boundary.

## Proxy controls

- Port `8080` binds only to loopback.
- mitmproxy is restricted to TLS interception of `api.anthropic.com`.
- `authorization`, `cookie`, `set-cookie`, `x-api-key`, and proxy authorization headers are replaced before proxy events are written.
- Sensitive query fields are replaced.
- The project CA is not installed in the macOS system trust store. Claude receives its path through `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` only while activation is enabled.
- The CA private key under `data/mitmproxy/` must be treated as a credential.

Body content is not redacted in raw proxy events. A user can put a secret directly in a prompt or tool result.

## Settings mutation

`enable` modifies only the `env` object in Claude's user `settings.json` and records:

- An exact pre-change backup.
- Original presence/value for every managed key.
- Before/after SHA-256 values.

It fails when an existing managed value conflicts unless `--force` is supplied. `disable` restores only managed keys and preserves unrelated settings added later. It fails if a managed value changed after activation rather than overwriting the new value.

The tool does not automatically restart, terminate, or sign out Claude Desktop.

## Derived redacted exports

`export-redacted` creates a separate tree and never overwrites raw evidence. It applies field-name redaction and common token-shape redaction, but it is not a proof that all secrets have been removed. Review derived exports before sharing them.

## Retention

Collector files rotate at bounded sizes and retain rotated backups for 14 days. Active run data, raw API-body files, transcripts, settings backups, proxy CA material, snapshots, and exports remain until the operator deliberately removes them.             },

        self.assertNotIn("abcdefghijklmnop", redacted)

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import tempfile
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

from openbox_logger.settings import SettingsError, activate, deactivate


class SettingsTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        self.temporary = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
        self.addCleanup(self.temporary.cleanup)
        self.root = Path(self.temporary.name) / "project"
        self.root.mkdir()
        self.settings = Path(self.temporary.name) / "claude/settings.json"
        self.settings.parent.mkdir()

    def write_settings(self, value: dict) -> None:
        self.settings.write_text(json.dumps(value) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    def read_settings(self) -> dict:
        return json.loads(self.settings.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    def test_activate_and_deactivate_preserve_unrelated_changes(self) -> None:
        self.write_settings({"theme": "dark", "env": {"EXISTING": "yes"}})
        state = activate(self.root, proxy=False, settings_path=self.settings)
        active = self.read_settings()
        self.assertEqual(active["env"]["CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY"], "1")
        self.assertTrue(Path(state["backup_path"]).is_file())

        active["new_setting"] = "created-later"
        active["env"]["UNRELATED_AFTER_ENABLE"] = "keep"
        self.write_settings(active)
        deactivate(self.root, settings_path=self.settings)

        restored = self.read_settings()
        self.assertEqual(restored["theme"], "dark")
        self.assertEqual(restored["new_setting"], "created-later")
        self.assertEqual(restored["env"], {"EXISTING": "yes", "UNRELATED_AFTER_ENABLE": "keep"})

    def test_conflicting_value_fails_closed(self) -> None:
        self.write_settings({"env": {"OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER": "console"}})
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(SettingsError, "conflict"):
            activate(self.root, proxy=False, settings_path=self.settings)
        self.assertEqual(self.read_settings()["env"]["OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER"], "console")

    def test_proxy_requires_ca_and_merges_no_proxy(self) -> None:
        self.write_settings({"env": {"NO_PROXY": "example.internal"}})
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(SettingsError, "proxy CA"):
            activate(self.root, proxy=True, settings_path=self.settings)
        ca = self.root / "data/mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem"
        ca.parent.mkdir(parents=True)
        ca.write_text("test-ca", encoding="utf-8")
        activate(self.root, proxy=True, settings_path=self.settings)
        no_proxy = self.read_settings()["env"]["NO_PROXY"].split(",")
        self.assertEqual(no_proxy, ["example.internal", "localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1"])
        deactivate(self.root, settings_path=self.settings)
        self.assertEqual(self.read_settings()["env"]["NO_PROXY"], "example.internal")

    def test_disable_refuses_changed_managed_value(self) -> None:
        self.write_settings({})
        activate(self.root, proxy=False, settings_path=self.settings)
        changed = self.read_settings()
        changed["env"]["OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER"] = "console"
        self.write_settings(changed)
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(SettingsError, "changed after activation"):
            deactivate(self.root, settings_path=self.settings)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

import json
import tempfile
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

from openbox_logger.transcripts import TranscriptWatcher, import_history


class TranscriptWatcherTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        self.temporary = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
        self.addCleanup(self.temporary.cleanup)
        self.root = Path(self.temporary.name)
        self.source = self.root / "projects"
        self.source.mkdir()
        self.output = self.root / "capture/events.jsonl"
        self.cursor = self.root / "capture/cursor.json"

    @staticmethod
    def line(event_type: str, text: str) -> str:
        return (
            json.dumps(
                {
                    "type": event_type,
                    "sessionId": "session-1",
                    "message": {"content": text},
                }
            )
            + "\n"
        )

    def events(self) -> list[dict]:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in self.output.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()]

    def test_seed_skips_history_then_captures_append(self) -> None:
        transcript = self.source / "session-1.jsonl"
        transcript.write_text(self.line("user", "old"), encoding="utf-8")
        watcher = TranscriptWatcher(self.source, self.output, self.cursor)
        watcher.seed_from_end()
        transcript.write_text(
            self.line("user", "old") + self.line("assistant", "new"),
            encoding="utf-8",
        )
        self.assertEqual(watcher.poll_once(), 1)
        captured = self.events()
        self.assertEqual(captured[0]["kind"], "transcript.assistant")
        self.assertEqual(captured[0]["payload"]["message"]["content"], "new")

    def test_new_file_is_captured_from_start(self) -> None:
        watcher = TranscriptWatcher(self.source, self.output, self.cursor)
        watcher.seed_from_end()
        nested = self.source / "project/session/subagents"
        nested.mkdir(parents=True)
        (nested / "agent.jsonl").write_text(self.line("user", "new file"), encoding="utf-8")
        self.assertEqual(watcher.poll_once(), 1)
        self.assertIn("subagents/agent.jsonl", self.events()[0]["source_file"])

    def test_partial_line_waits_for_newline(self) -> None:
        transcript = self.source / "partial.jsonl"
        transcript.write_text("", encoding="utf-8")
        watcher = TranscriptWatcher(self.source, self.output, self.cursor)
        watcher.seed_from_end()
        payload = self.line("user", "complete")
        transcript.write_text(payload.rstrip("\n"), encoding="utf-8")
        self.assertEqual(watcher.poll_once(), 0)
        with transcript.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write("\n")
        self.assertEqual(watcher.poll_once(), 1)

    def test_history_import_is_explicit_and_complete(self) -> None:
        source_fixture = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures/transcript.jsonl"
        (self.source / "fixture.jsonl").write_bytes(source_fixture.read_bytes())
        self.assertEqual(import_history(self.source, self.output), 2)

Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on - the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves - and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes - the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on - no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` - no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end - never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11-13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool - simplify instead.

  <h1>OpenBox Logger Teardown</h1>
  <p class="standfirst">A local, reversible observation stack for authorized Claude Desktop <strong>Code → Local</strong> sessions. ~1,690 lines of Python plus two pinned containers. Its whole design argument is that <strong>no single log is the truth</strong> — so it captures three independent evidence lanes and gives you the keys to join them.</p>

<section id="thesis">
  <h2><span class="num">01</span>The thesis: no lane is “all the messages”</h2>
  <p class="lede">Most logging tools pick one vantage point and call it complete. This one refuses to, and the refusal is the architecture.</p>

  <p>Ask “what did Claude actually do?” and there are three honest answers, each incomplete:</p>

  <ul>
    <li>The <strong>transcript</strong> is what Claude chose to persist to disk — assembled, post-hoc, authoritative about conversation state and nothing else.</li>
    <li>The <strong>telemetry</strong> is what Claude chose to instrument — permission decisions, tool timings, token costs, and (opt-in) the untruncated Messages API bodies. Richest lane, but it exists only because Claude emits it.</li>
    <li>The <strong>proxy</strong> is what actually crossed the wire — the only lane that doesn't take Claude's word for anything, and the only one that requires TLS interception to get.</li>
  </ul>

  <p>The project is explicit about the ceiling, too. <a href="#">docs/CAPTURE_MODEL.md</a> lists what <em>cannot</em> be seen: hidden extended thinking (redacted upstream), server-internal processing, Desktop UI-only state, and the local IPC hop between the Desktop UI and its embedded engine. Cloud and SSH sessions are out of scope entirely — a proxy on this Mac never sees them.</p>

  <div class="callout">
    <p class="h">What this collects</p>
    <p>Complete conversation history, file contents, shell output, MCP results, and any credential a user pasted into a prompt. The raw lanes are <em>deliberately</em> unredacted because they are evidence. Only headers, cookies, and secret-shaped query values are stripped. Treat <code>data/</code> as you would a production database dump.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="lanes">
  <h2><span class="num">03</span>The three lanes, concretely</h2>
  <p class="lede">What each lane actually contained during the live run I inspected.</p>

  <div class="lanes">
    <div class="lane t">
      <span class="tag">Lane 1 · native</span>
      <h4>Transcript</h4>
      <p>Claude's own persisted JSONL, tailed by byte offset and re-enveloped. Payload is passed through <em>whole</em> — the watcher adds provenance, never edits content.</p>
      <dl>
        <div><dt>writer</dt><dd>host python</dd></div>
        <div><dt>kind</dt><dd>transcript.<type></dd></div>
        <div><dt>seen</dt><dd>assistant, user, attachment, last-prompt, bridge-session, queue-operation</dd></div>
        <div><dt>keys</dt><dd>session_id, source_file, source_offset</dd></div>
      </dl>
    </div>
    <div class="lane o">
      <span class="tag">Lane 2 · instrumented</span>
      <h4>OpenTelemetry</h4>
      <p>Canonical OTLP JSON, deliberately <em>not</em> reshaped into the project's schema so no upstream field is lost. Richest lane by far.</p>
      <dl>
        <div><dt>writer</dt><dd>collector container</dd></div>
        <div><dt>logs</dt><dd>user_prompt, tool_decision, tool_result, api_request, api_request_body, assistant_response, mcp_server_connection, hook_execution_*</dd></div>
        <div><dt>traces</dt><dd>claude_code.interaction ▸ .llm_request ▸ .tool ▸ .tool.execution</dd></div>
        <div><dt>metrics</dt><dd>token.usage, cost.usage, session.count, active_time.total</dd></div>
      </dl>
    </div>
    <div class="lane p">
      <span class="tag">Lane 3 · optional · invasive</span>
      <h4>Proxy transport</h4>
      <p>The real HTTP. Only lane that is independent of Claude's cooperation, and the only one needing a CA. Restricted by regex to a single host.</p>
      <dl>
        <div><dt>writer</dt><dd>mitmproxy container</dd></div>
        <div><dt>kind</dt><dd>proxy.request / .response / .error</dd></div>
        <div><dt>endpoints</dt><dd>/v1/messages, /messages/count_tokens, /v1/code/sessions/…/worker/*, event_logging/v2/batch</dd></div>
        <div><dt>keys</dt><dd>flow_id, request_id, session_id (partial)</dd></div>
      </dl>
    </div>
  </div>

<section id="start">
  <h2><span class="num">05</span>Sequence: <code>start --proxy</code></h2>
  <p class="lede">A gated startup with full rollback. Every wait has a deadline, and any failure tears the whole thing back down and marks the run <code>failed</code> rather than leaving half a stack up.</p>

  <figure class="plate">
    <p class="fig-label">Figure 3</p>
    <div class="scroll">

    </div>
    <figcaption><b>Gate, then commit.</b> The run is only marked <code>active</code> after four independent readiness proofs: collector HTTP health, proxy TCP accept, CA file existence, and a watcher-written <code>watcher.ready</code> sentinel. The rollback block is a single <code>except</code> around the whole sequence — there is no partial-success state.</figcaption>
  </figure>

  <p>Two details worth noting. The watcher is spawned via <code>start_new_session=True</code>, so it survives the CLI exiting — it is a detached host process, not a container. And <code>--profile proxy</code> is passed on <em>every</em> compose invocation, including <code>down</code> and <code>ps</code>; without it, the proxy service would be invisible to teardown.</p>
</section>

  <p>To reconstruct one model call end to end: take <code>prompt.id</code> from the <code>user_prompt</code> log record, collect every OTel record sharing it, follow <code>api_request_body.body_ref</code> to the request JSON on disk, take <code>request_id</code> from the sibling <code>api_request</code> record, use it to fetch the response JSON <em>and</em> to find the matching <code>proxy.response</code>, then use that event's <code>flow_id</code> to recover the corresponding <code>proxy.request</code>. Confirm against the transcript via <code>session.id</code>.</p>

<section id="layout">
  <h2><span class="num">10</span>Data layout and what is per-run</h2>
  <p class="lede">The split between run-scoped and global is the layout's one sharp edge.</p>

  <pre class="code"><code>data/                            0700, git-ignored except .gitkeep
├── runs/<run-id>/                ← PER RUN
│   ├── run.json                  status: starting → active → stopped | failed
│   ├── watcher.log / .ready      stdout of the detached watcher; readiness sentinel
│   ├── transcripts/
│   │   ├── events.jsonl          0600 · normalized transcript envelopes
│   │   └── cursor.json           per-file {offset, inode}, 346 entries
│   ├── otel/{logs,traces,metrics}.jsonl   0640 · canonical OTLP, rotates
│   └── proxy/events.jsonl        0644 · transport events, NO rotation
├── api-bodies/                   ← GLOBAL · written by Claude, mode 0644
├── backups/                      exact settings.json copies, before + after
├── mitmproxy/                    project CA — the .pem key is a credential
├── exports/                      snapshots and derived redacted trees
├── state/current-run.json        the one pointer every command reads
└── state/activation.json         the undo record for settings</code></pre>

  <p>Only <code>data/runs/<run-id>/</code> is partitioned by run. <code>api-bodies/</code> accumulates across every run forever, which is why <code>export-redacted</code> has to name it as a second explicit source alongside the run directory. Both <code>report</code> and <code>snapshot</code> deliberately skip <code>backups/</code> so your own settings history never lands in an evidence manifest.</p>

  <h3>Evidence integrity</h3>
  <p><code>snapshot</code> walks <code>data/</code> and writes <code>{path, bytes, sha256}</code> for every file into a timestamped manifest — 26 files in the one already in <code>exports/</code>. <code>export-redacted</code> builds a <em>separate</em> tree, applying recursive key-name redaction (<code>authorization</code>, <code>api_key</code>, <code>token</code>, <code>password</code>, <code>secret</code>, <code>private_key</code>, …) plus value-shape patterns for <code>Bearer</code>, <code>sk-ant-</code>, <code>ghp_</code>/<code>github_pat_</code>, and <code>AKIA</code>. Raw evidence is never modified in place. The docs are honest that this is not a proof of secret removal.</p>

  <p>Every host-side write goes through the same primitive: <code>mkstemp</code> → write → <code>fsync</code> → <code>chmod</code> → <code>os.replace</code>. Interrupt a command and you get either the old file or the new one, never a truncated one.</p>
</section>

<section id="reverse">
  <h2><span class="num">11</span>Reversibility, precisely</h2>
  <p class="lede">The claim is “restores only keys it manages.” That claim is tested, and the test is a good one.</p>

  <p><code>test_activate_and_deactivate_preserve_unrelated_changes</code> enables capture, then simulates a user editing settings <em>afterwards</em> — adding a new top-level key and a new unrelated <code>env</code> var — and asserts that <code>disable</code> keeps both while removing exactly the 19 managed keys. Restoration is driven by the recorded <code>original</code> map: a key that was absent before is deleted, a key that had a value gets that value back. If <code>env</code> did not exist at all before, the whole object is removed again.</p>

  <div class="tw">
    <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Situation</th><th>Behavior</th><th>Override</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Managed key already set to a different value</td><td><code>enable</code> aborts, names the conflicts, writes nothing</td><td class="mono">--force</td></tr>
        <tr><td>A managed value changed after activation</td><td><code>disable</code> refuses rather than clobbering the newer value</td><td class="mono">--force</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Settings already active</td><td><code>enable</code> refuses a second activation</td><td class="no">none</td></tr>
        <tr><td>A run is already <code>starting</code>/<code>active</code></td><td><code>start</code> refuses</td><td class="no">none</td></tr>
        <tr><td><code>enable --proxy</code> before the CA exists</td><td>Aborts with the path it expected</td><td class="no">none</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Recorded watcher PID is not the watcher</td><td><code>stop</code> refuses to signal it</td><td class="no">none</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Historical transcripts</td><td>Skipped; <code>import-history</code> aborts without confirmation</td><td class="mono">--yes</td></tr>
        <tr><td><code>stop</code> / <code>disable</code></td><td>Never delete captured data</td><td class="no">manual only</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>The PID guard deserves a mention: <code>stop</code> shells out to <code>ps -p <pid> -o command=</code> and refuses to send a signal unless the command line contains both <code>openbox-logger</code> and <code>_watch</code>. That closes the PID-reuse hole where a recycled PID could get SIGTERM'd. It then escalates SIGTERM → SIGKILL with a 5s grace.</p>
</section>

<section id="findings">
  <h2><span class="num">12</span>Findings from the live capture</h2>
  <p class="lede">Things I verified against <code>data/</code> that the docs either don't say or understate. Ordered by how likely they are to bite you.</p>

  <div class="finding high">
    <h4><span class="sev">operational</span>The proxy lane has no size bound</h4>
    <p>The collector's file exporter rotates at 64 MB with 14-day retention. <code>capture.py</code> just opens the file in append mode — no rotation, no cap. In the run I inspected, <code>proxy/events.jsonl</code> reached 27 MB in about 13 minutes of ordinary use, and every response body is stored in full.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> 19.5 MB at first read, 27.7 MB eight minutes later; 998 events. <b>Implies</b> ≈ 2 MB/min, ≈ 125 MB/hour. Watch the disk on long runs, or prefer the non-proxy default.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding high">
    <h4><span class="sev">gotcha</span>Proxy bodies are captured compressed, so the interesting ones aren't readable</h4>
    <p><code>capture.py</code> reads <code>flow.request.raw_content</code> / <code>flow.response.raw_content</code> — the bytes as they crossed the wire, <em>before</em> content-encoding is undone. Requests are uncompressed JSON and read fine. Responses are not: <code>/v1/messages</code> comes back gzipped SSE or brotli JSON, so those land as <code>{"encoding":"base64"}</code> blobs. <code>docs/SCHEMA.md</code> describes them as “the full assembled response transport body” without noting you must decompress to read one.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> all 46 <code>/v1/messages</code> responses base64 — 24 <code>gzip; text/event-stream</code>, 22 <code>br; application/json</code>. Lane-wide: 472 base64, 445 json, 70 utf-8. <b>Note</b> mitmproxy's <code>.content</code> would decode automatically; <code>raw_content</code> is arguably the right choice for transport fidelity, but the tradeoff is undocumented. The OTel <code>api-bodies</code> lane gives you the same payloads as plain JSON.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding med">
    <h4><span class="sev">scope</span>The proxy is process-wide, not run-scoped or session-scoped</h4>
    <p><code>HTTP_PROXY</code> applies to everything the Claude engine sends to <code>api.anthropic.com</code>. The capture therefore includes token counting, settings and policy fetches, event-logging batches, and worker heartbeats for Claude Code <em>cloud</em> sessions — I saw two distinct <code>cse_…</code> session identifiers in the traffic — alongside the local session you meant to observe.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> top endpoints by volume were <code>/v1/messages/count_tokens</code> (87), <code>/v1/code/sessions/<cse_…>/worker/internal-events</code> (45), <code>/v1/messages</code> (42). <b>Consequence:</b> filter by endpoint before treating the lane as one session's transport.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding med">
    <h4><span class="sev">privacy</span>File modes are inconsistent across the three writers</h4>
    <p>The project's own writes are <code>0600</code>. The collector writes <code>0640</code>. The two lanes holding the <em>most</em> sensitive payloads are the loosest: <code>proxy/events.jsonl</code> is <code>0644</code> (the addon opens the file without a chmod) and <code>api-bodies/*.json</code> is <code>0644</code> (Claude writes those, so the project has no say). The parent <code>data/</code> directory is <code>0700</code>, which blocks traversal by other local users, so this is a defense-in-depth gap rather than an open door — but the file modes don't match the project's stated convention.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> <code>transcripts/events.jsonl</code> <code>-rw-------</code>; <code>otel/logs.jsonl</code> <code>-rw-r-----</code>; <code>proxy/events.jsonl</code> <code>-rw-r--r--</code>; <code>api-bodies/*.json</code> <code>-rw-r--r--</code>. <b>SECURITY.md</b> hedges this correctly — “where the host process controls creation.”</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding med">
    <h4><span class="sev">correlation</span><code>session_id</code> is absent from most proxy events</h4>
    <p><code>CAPTURE_MODEL.md</code> lists <code>X-Claude-Code-Session-Id</code> as a correlation key, and it is retained where present — but most endpoints don't send it, so the field is <code>null</code> on the majority of events.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> 288 of 998 events carried it; 710 were <code>null</code>. <b>Use</b> <code>request_id</code> as the primary transcript↔proxy bridge instead — that matched 25/25 in my check.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding info">
    <h4><span class="sev">footgun</span><code>doctor</code> reports not-ready if <code>jq</code> is missing</h4>
    <p><code>doctor</code> checks for <code>docker</code>, <code>python3</code>, and <code>jq</code>, and computes <code>ready</code> as the AND of every check — so a missing <code>jq</code> makes the command exit 1. No Python module in the project actually uses <code>jq</code>; it is a convenience for reading the JSONL by hand.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Present here:</b> <code>/opt/homebrew/bin/jq</code>, so <code>doctor</code> passes. On a machine without it, the gate fails for a dependency nothing needs.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding info">
    <h4><span class="sev">scope</span>Capture spans every project on the machine</h4>
    <p>Covered in §08, repeated here because it is a consent question, not just a mechanic: the watcher tails all of <code>~/.claude/projects</code>. This run tracked 346 transcript files and actively recorded two unrelated repositories at once.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Evidence:</b> <code>cursor.json</code> holds 346 entries; captured events came from <code>-Users-phuongvu-Code-openbox-openbox-logger/</code> and <code>-Users-phuongvu-Code-openbox-openbox-backend/</code>.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="finding info">
    <h4><span class="sev">note</span>OTel attributes carry account identity on every record</h4>
    <p>Not a defect — it is what the upstream telemetry emits, and it is genuinely useful for attribution. Worth knowing before you share a lane: every log record and span repeats <code>user.email</code>, <code>user.account_uuid</code>, <code>user.account_id</code>, <code>organization.id</code>, and a hashed <code>user.id</code>, alongside <code>os.version</code> and <code>process.owner</code>.</p>
    <p class="ev"><b>Note</b> <code>export-redacted</code>'s key patterns do not match <code>user.email</code> or <code>organization.id</code>, so these survive into a redacted export. Review before sharing.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="commands">
  <h2><span class="num">13</span>Command reference</h2>
  <p class="lede">Every command is a <code>make</code> target or a direct <code>./bin/openbox-logger</code> call. The binary is a four-line shim that puts <code>src/</code> on the path and calls <code>cli.main</code>.</p>

  <div class="tw">
    <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Command</th><th>Mutates</th><th>Notes</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td class="mono">init</td><td>data/ only</td><td>Creates seven <code>0700</code> directories. Idempotent.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">doctor [--json]</td><td class="no">nothing</td><td>Docker + daemon, python3, jq, Claude.app version via Info.plist, transcripts dir, embedded Claude Code version sniffed from recent JSONL, settings parse. Exit 1 if any check fails.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">start [--proxy]</td><td>containers, watcher</td><td>Mints the run-id. Does <em>not</em> touch Claude settings.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">enable [--proxy] [--force]</td><td>~/.claude/settings.json</td><td>Does <em>not</em> start anything. Requires a Claude restart.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">status [--json]</td><td class="no">nothing</td><td>Watcher liveness, three port probes, <code>compose ps</code>, and a redacted activation summary — managed key <em>names</em> only, never values.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">tail --source {transcript,proxy}</td><td class="no">nothing</td><td>Default 20 lines, tab-separated <code>observed_at · source · kind · session_id</code>. <code>--json</code> prints whole events.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">report [--json]</td><td class="no">nothing</td><td>Sizes, record counts, invalid-JSON counts, and a histogram of transcript <code>kind</code>s. No message content. Skips <code>backups/</code>.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">snapshot [--output]</td><td>writes a manifest</td><td>SHA-256 of every file under <code>data/</code>.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">export-redacted [--output]</td><td>writes a new tree</td><td>Derived copy of the current run plus <code>api-bodies/</code>. Raw data untouched.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">import-history --yes</td><td>writes to exports/</td><td>Reads all history with a zeroed cursor. Refuses without <code>--yes</code>.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">disable [--force]</td><td>~/.claude/settings.json</td><td>Restores managed keys; writes a second backup first.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">stop</td><td>containers, watcher</td><td>Retains all data.</td></tr>
        <tr><td class="mono">_watch --run-id</td><td>writes the transcript lane</td><td>Hidden. The watcher body; spawned by <code>start</code>, not for direct use.</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <h3>Verification</h3>
  <p><code>make test</code> runs 13 unittest cases with no network and no Docker — settings activate/deactivate round-trips, the watcher's seed/partial-line/new-file behaviors, redaction, and the proxy addon's sanitizers. The addon is imported by file path with <code>importlib</code>, and it guards its own <code>mitmproxy</code> import so it loads on a host without mitmproxy installed. <code>make validate</code> goes further: <code>compileall</code>, <code>docker compose config</code>, and the pinned collector image validating its own config — without enabling capture.</p>
</section>

<footer class="end">
  <p>Read at commit <code>097ff1f</code> on branch <code>main</code>, working tree clean. Counts and file modes were sampled from a live <code>active</code> run (<code>20260827T063932Z-225cac</code>, proxy on) and will differ in yours. Container liveness could not be probed directly from this session — the Docker socket was outside the sandbox — but the OTel, proxy, and transcript files were all being written during the read, which is the same proof by other means.</p>
  <p>Open questions, none blocking: is <code>raw_content</code> in <code>capture.py</code> a deliberate transport-fidelity choice (and worth a line in <code>SCHEMA.md</code>) or an oversight? Should the proxy lane get the collector's rotation treatment? Should the watcher accept a project filter, given that a run currently observes every Claude session on the machine?</p>
</footer>

</main>
